title: Independence of the polynomial presentation for Koszul-regular kernels
statement: For an ideal $L$ in a commutative ring $T$, say that $L$ is locally Koszul-regular if for every prime $\mathfrak a\subset T$ containing $L$ there are $u\in T\setminus\mathfrak a$, $r\geq0$, and $a_1,\ldots,a_r\in T_u$ with $LT_u=(a_1,\ldots,a_r)$ and $H_i(K_\bullet(T_u;a_1,\ldots,a_r))=0$ for all $i>0$ [def-weil-ring-localization-away, def-weil-pbc-koszul-regular-sequence]. Let $R,S$ be commutative rings with an $R$-algebra structure on $S$, and let $\alpha:R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\twoheadrightarrow S$ and $\beta:R[y_1,\ldots,y_m]\twoheadrightarrow S$ be surjective $R$-algebra maps with $n,m\geq0$ [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring]. If $\ker\alpha$ is locally Koszul-regular, then $\ker\beta$ is locally Koszul-regular. No flatness or Noetherian hypothesis is imposed. The zero algebra and zero-variable presentations are allowed.

proof.text: Write $P=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$, $Q=R[y_1,\ldots,y_m]$, $C=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n,y_1,\ldots,y_m]$, $I=\ker\alpha$, $J=\ker\beta$. Choose $f_j\in P$ and $g_i\in Q$ lifting $\beta(y_j)$ and $\alpha(x_i)$ respectively. Evaluation gives $e_y:C\to P$, $y_j\mapsto f_j$, and $e_x:C\to Q$, $x_i\mapsto g_i$. The common map $\gamma=\alpha e_y=\beta e_x$ is surjective. Its kernel satisfies $K=(I,y_j-f_j)=(J,x_i-g_i)$: subtracting the evaluated polynomial leaves a sum of multiples of the differences (apply $T^d-a^d=(T-a)\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}T^{d-1-k}a^k$ successively to each monomial). This also identifies $C/(y_j-f_j)=P$ and $C/(x_i-g_i)=Q$.

source.place: Tag 07CZ (lemma-koszul-independence-presentation), proof; primewise refinement avoiding global finite generation.

proof.text: Fix a prime $\mathfrak q\subset S$ and write $\mathfrak p=\alpha^{-1}(\mathfrak q)$, $\mathfrak r=\beta^{-1}(\mathfrak q)$, $\mathfrak t=\gamma^{-1}(\mathfrak q)$. Choose $u\in P\setminus\mathfrak p$ and a Koszul-regular tuple $a_1,\ldots,a_t$ generating $I_u$ in $P_u$. In $C_u=P_u[y_1,\ldots,y_m]$, the graph tuple $d=(y_j-f_j)$ is weakly regular: translation $y_j\mapsto y_j+f_j$ identifies each successive quotient and multiplication with a polynomial variable, which is injective by comparison of coefficients. Hence $d$ is Koszul-regular by the cited weak-regular-to-Koszul theorem. Its quotient is $P_u$, where $a$ is Koszul-regular. The prefix criterion now makes $(d,a)$ Koszul-regular in $C_u$, generating $K_u$, of length $m+t$.

source.place: Tag 07CZ (lemma-koszul-independence-presentation), proof; primewise refinement avoiding global finite generation.

proof.text: Set $v=e_x(u)=u(g_1,\ldots,g_n)\in Q$. Since $\beta(v)=\alpha(u)\notin\mathfrak q$, $v\notin\mathfrak r$. The surjection $e_x:C_u\twoheadrightarrow Q_v$ sends $K_u$ onto $J_v$: for an element of $J_v$ lift its numerator through $C\to Q$; its image under $\gamma$ is zero. Thus $J_v$ is generated by the finitely many images of $(d,a)$. In particular $J_v$ is finite as a $Q_v$-module. This proves precisely the finite generation needed near $\mathfrak r$, without assuming that $J$ is globally finite.

source.place: Tag 07CZ (lemma-koszul-independence-presentation), proof; primewise refinement avoiding global finite generation.

proof.text: Use $\kappa= S_{\mathfrak q}/\mathfrak qS_{\mathfrak q}$, also the residue field at $\mathfrak p$ or $\mathfrak r$. The conormal-basis theorem for $a$ in $P_u$ gives $\dim_\kappa((I/I^2)\otimes_S\kappa)=t$. Put $s=\dim_\kappa((J/J^2)\otimes_S\kappa)$, finite by step 3. The stable conormal isomorphism, applied to $\alpha,\beta$ with localization element $1$, and then tensored with $\kappa$, yields $t+m=s+n$. Here $(I/I^2)\otimes_S\kappa=I\otimes_P\kappa$ and $(J/J^2)\otimes_S\kappa=J\otimes_Q\kappa$: the squares vanish because $I\subset\mathfrak p$, $J\subset\mathfrak r$. Localization at $u$ or $v$ changes none of these fibres since their images in $\kappa$ are units.

source.place: Tag 07CZ (lemma-koszul-independence-presentation), proof; primewise refinement avoiding global finite generation.

proof.text: Choose $b_1,\ldots,b_s\in J$ whose images form a $\kappa$-basis of $J\otimes_Q\kappa$: the images of a finite generating set of $J_v$ span, so select a basis from them and multiply each chosen fraction by a power of $v$ to obtain elements of $J$ (nonzero scalar rescaling preserves a basis). Nakayama applied to the finite module $J_{\mathfrak r}$ over $Q_{\mathfrak r}$ says that these $b_j$ generate $J_{\mathfrak r}$. For each member $z_l$ of a finite generating set of $J_v$, express $z_l$ as a combination of the $b_j$ in $J_{\mathfrak r}$, clear the finitely many coefficient denominators, and multiply by a further element outside $\mathfrak r$ killing the equality error. The product $w\in Q\setminus\mathfrak r$ of all these elements makes $J_{vw}=(b_1,\ldots,b_s)$. This is valid for $s=0$ too: the finitely many generators are then all killed after that localization.

source.place: Tag 07CZ (lemma-koszul-independence-presentation), proof; primewise refinement avoiding global finite generation.

proof.text: Pass to $D=C_{u v w}$, where $v,w$ are viewed as polynomials in the $y$ variables. Localizations are flat, so $(d,a)$ remains Koszul-regular there. It generates $KD$. The other kernel formula and step 5 show that $KD$ is also generated by $(x_1-g_1,\ldots,x_n-g_n,b_1,\ldots,b_s)$. These two tuples have equal length $m+t=n+s$. The equal-length-generator lemma therefore makes the latter tuple Koszul-regular in $D$.

source.place: Tag 07CZ (lemma-koszul-independence-presentation), proof; primewise refinement avoiding global finite generation.

proof.text: The prefix $c=(x_1-g_1,\ldots,x_n-g_n)$ is Koszul-regular already in $C=Q[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$: translation identifies it with the variables, whose successive multiplications are injective coefficientwise, and the weak-regular-to-Koszul theorem applies. It remains Koszul-regular in $D$ by flat localization. Apply the reverse direction of the prefix criterion to $(c,b)$ in $D$. Thus the images of $b_1,\ldots,b_s$ are Koszul-regular in $D/(c)$.

source.place: Tag 07CZ (lemma-koszul-independence-presentation), proof; primewise refinement avoiding global finite generation.

proof.text: The evaluation quotient from step 1 identifies $D/(c)$ with $Q_{v^2w}=Q_{vw}$: the image of $u$ is $v$, so the product inverted is $v^2w$; inverting $v^2w$ and inverting $vw$ have the same universal property. Under this isomorphism the tuple remains $b_1,\ldots,b_s$, which generates $J_{vw}$ by step 5. Since $vw\notin\mathfrak r$, this gives the required principal neighborhood at $\mathfrak r$. Every prime containing $J$ is the inverse image of a prime of $S=Q/J$, so all required primes have been covered. If $S=0$ there are no such primes and the assertion is vacuous. Empty variable sets or tuples use the same formulas and impose no excluded case.

source.place: Tag 07CZ (lemma-koszul-independence-presentation), proof; primewise refinement avoiding global finite generation.

tool_uses.why: Weakly regular graph-variable tuples are Koszul-regular without a proper-ideal hypothesis; this is a general ring-theoretic tool.
The conormal classes of the regular generators give the exact local generator count t.
At localization element 1, the stable conormal isomorphism compares the two finite polynomial presentations and gives the length equality.
Nakayama for the finite localized ideal gives generation by residue-field basis lifts.
Flat localization preserves Koszul-regular sequences; no statement in this unit replaces this general tool.
